items.question: Who specifically is this two-volume book written for?
items.answer: “Orangutan +3” is written specifically for CEOs, factory owners, workshop founders, senior operations officers, and business owners in developing markets. If you feel the entire decision-making weight rests on your shoulders or output drops whenever you leave, this book is your exact roadmap.
highlights: CEOs and owners of manufacturing and service industries
Senior executive, financial, and commercial directors
Entrepreneurs seeking to transition from emotional management to sustainable structure

items.question: Is an MBA or academic background required to understand the content?
items.answer: No! The language is practical, direct, and free of overly academic jargon. All models, formulas, and decision cards were distilled from real experience on factory floors and Iranian enterprises.
highlights: Simple language, free from unpractical theoretical fluff
Focused on native examples and real market challenges
Step-by-step actionable checklists and protocols

items.question: What is the primary difference between Volume 1 and Volume 2?
items.answer: Volume 1 (From Instinctive Management to Self-Awareness) diagnoses and unmasks instinctive decision traps, revealing the root causes of financial leaks. Volume 2 (Sustainability & Growth Roadmap +3) provides operational tools, triple levers, decision cards, and learning architecture so the system runs independently.
highlights: Vol 1: Pathology and recognition of instinctive decision traps
Vol 2: Tool building, waste formulas, and sustainable structure

items.question: Why is this book different from translated Western management books?
items.answer: Most management books on the market are translations of Western texts that ignore local economic conditions, high inflation, currency shifts, and workforce culture. Orangutan +3 comes directly from 40 years of hands-on industrial practice.
highlights: Adapted to inflation and volatile market environments
In-depth analysis of native workforce culture and organizational behavior
Covers real case studies from local manufacturing sectors

framework.title: Interactive 3+ Framework Simulator
framework.subtitle: Ali Asghar Hakimian's 3-step formula to rescue organizations from instinctive behaviors, repeated errors, and absolute reliance on personal memory.
framework.bottomText: All 3+ Framework stages with real formulas and operational checklists are detailed in Volume 1 and Volume 2.

steps.title: Unfiltered Reality Observation
steps.subtitle: Moving beyond polished reports to direct shop-floor observation
steps.description: Most managers view their organization from behind smoked-glass office windows. Financial reports and stats usually arrive retouched and delayed. In Step 1 of 3+, managers learn to go directly to production, warehouse, and customer touchpoints to analyze live data firsthand.
steps.orangutanDiff: In instinctive mode, the manager simply shouts and blames based on gut feeling.
steps.plus3Diff: In the 3+ Framework, the manager identifies root causes using first-hand shop-floor data.

steps.title: Leverage Point Intervention
steps.subtitle: Focusing on the primary bottleneck (Theory of Constraints - TOC)
steps.description: Pressuring all departments simultaneously drains organizational energy. The leverage point is the bottleneck where a 10% improvement doubles total capacity—such as discovering the altitude effect at 2,143m in the whey powder case study.
steps.orangutanDiff: In instinctive mode, the manager pressures everyone, exhausting productive employees.
steps.plus3Diff: In the 3+ Framework, all organizational resources focus on resolving the true bottleneck.

steps.title: Institutionalization in Memory
steps.subtitle: Converting solutions into methods, checklists, and enduring training
steps.description: If a solution vanishes when a key person leaves, it is not a solution—it's a temporary painkiller. Institutionalization means drafting checklists, refining warehouse formulas, standardizing shelf addresses, and turning managers into systemizing teachers.
steps.orangutanDiff: In instinctive mode, when a key employee leaves, all knowledge and processes perish.
steps.plus3Diff: In the 3+ Framework, knowledge is embedded into processes, keeping the organization self-learning.

steps.title: + Positive Aftershocks (+1)
steps.subtitle: Cascading positive effects of a correct decision across the value chain
steps.description: When a leverage point is correctly fixed, like a pebble in water, it creates positive waves: employee morale rises, waste drops, invisible financial leaks stop, and real profit emerges.
steps.orangutanDiff: In instinctive mode, raw decisions create negative aftershocks and new crises.
steps.plus3Diff: In the 3+ Framework, one structural correction unleashes a wave of value creation throughout the organization.

t1.title: Severe Orangutan Mode (Emotional & Instinctive Management)
t1.description: Your organization feels the pain and pressure but fails to identify root causes. Decisions rely on sixth sense, shouting, and personal memory. Repeated errors incur heavy costs.
t1.recommendation: Essential reading: Volume 1 (Chapters 1-4: Raw shop-floor observation & 4 AM strainer logs).

t2.title: Fluctuating Instinctive Management (Semi-Systemic with High Dependency)
t2.description: You have some forms and tools, but key employee absences cause severe disruption. Profits leak through warehouse voids and toxic sales invoices.
t2.recommendation: Study Volumes 1 & 2 (Warehouse coding, toxic invoice removal, and true profit formulas).

t3.title: On the Path to 3+ Systemization (Growing Organization)
t3.description: Most processes are transparent, but enduring success requires turning all know-how into live checklists and training manager-teachers across all levels.
t3.recommendation: Study Volume 2 (Chapters 39 & 40: Hall of 40 Mistakes and 40 Lessons).

t4.title: Self-Learning & Enduring 3+ Organization (Excellent)
t4.description: Congratulations! Your organization possesses enduring memory, uses live data, and doesn't rely on the physical presence of the CEO. You have successfully implemented 3+ Framework concepts.

questions.question: When a production line or project faces delays, what is the initial reaction of top executives?

options.text: Holding an emergency meeting, shouting at supervisors, and penalizing operators.
options.feedback: Instinctive behavior: Emotional reaction without shop-floor data analysis.

options.text: Mandating overtime for all departments without inspecting the delay's root cause.
options.feedback: Uniform pressure across all departments exhausting productive employees.

options.text: Heading directly to the production floor, examining the live bottleneck, and checking warehouse inputs.
options.feedback: Unfiltered reality observation (Step 1 of 3+): Direct data-driven observation.

questions.question: How is warehouse inventory and customer order data maintained in your organization?

options.text: Mostly in the senior warehouse keeper's head or manual notebooks only he understands.
options.feedback: Dangerous reliance on individual memory with no organizational memory.

options.text: In multiple Excel spreadsheets where each manager holds a conflicting version.
options.feedback: Data debt and multiple conflicting versions of truth.

options.text: In an integrated coded system with precise shelf addresses and cycle counting.
options.feedback: Transparent logging and enduring organizational memory (3+ Framework).

questions.question: What is your primary metric for evaluating and rewarding the sales team?

options.text: Number of daily phone calls and sheer routine activity.
options.feedback: Rewarding activity over results, leading to wasted time.

options.text: Total invoiced amount, even if based on long-term credit and risky checks.
options.feedback: Creating toxic invoices and failing to distinguish real sales from debt.

options.text: Actual cash collected in the bank account and customer repeat purchases.
options.feedback: Results-oriented metric ensuring financial cash flow health (3+ Framework).

questions.question: What happens when a key employee (e.g., technical manager or warehouse lead) resigns?

options.text: Total department paralysis and giving salary ransoms to keep them at all costs.
options.feedback: Organization held hostage by an individual due to lack of standard procedures.

options.text: Hastily hiring a replacement and enduring months of costly mistakes.
options.feedback: Failure to transfer knowledge and experience systematically.

options.text: Relative calmness, as all processes have live checklists and video documentation.
options.feedback: Learning organization documented according to the 3+ Framework.

questions.question: How is your company's annual profit calculated?

options.text: Based on year-end bank balance, ignoring raw material replacement inflation.
options.feedback: Fatal financial self-deception in inflationary economies.

options.text: Based on traditional accounting that mistakes property/inventory inflation for profit.
options.feedback: Failing to separate inflation gains from true operational profit.

options.text: Strictly separating asset inflation gains from true net operational sales profit.
options.feedback: Financial intelligence calculating true raw material replacement power (3+ Framework).

caseStudies.badge: Direct Experience from 40 Years of Industry
caseStudies.title: Industrial Case Studies Vault
caseStudies.subtitle: Documented case breakdowns of the steam needle, 68-year bearing warehouse, PVC shortage, and toxic invoices detailed in Volumes 1 & 2.

items.title: Steam Needle & Whey Powder
items.subtitle: Boosting evaporation line capacity from 2.5 to 6.135 tons/hour
items.problem: The whey powder factory was stuck at a low capacity of 2.5 tons/hr, with everyone blaming the boiler.
items.leverIntervention: Uncovering the impact of 2,143m elevation on boiling points, adjusting cooling towers, and modifying operator habits for steam needle calibration.
items.results: Line capacity increased 2.4x to 6.135 tons/hr without purchasing multi-billion equipment.
items.quote: “The problem wasn't a $1M boiler; it was a cheap needle adjustment and ignoring factory altitude.”

items.title: 8-Ton PVC Shortage & Internal Bleeding
items.subtitle: Exposing silent raw material leaks from the warehouse
items.problem: During year-end audit, 8 tons of PVC raw material went missing despite matching paperwork.
items.leverIntervention: Reconciling standard production formulas with waste logs and actual output weights, exposing scale calibration errors.
items.results: Preventing multi-billion annual losses and sealing material leaks with real-time logging.
items.quote: “Internal bleeding is fatal because the organization feels no immediate pain while slowly dying.”

items.title: 68-Year Bearing Warehouse Audit
items.subtitle: Overcoming absolute reliance on personal memory
items.problem: A 68-year-old enterprise with thousands of bearing parts located only in an old storekeeper's memory.
items.leverIntervention: Implementing open warehouse audits, unified part coding, 3D rack addresses, and cycle counting.
items.results: Line downtime dropped to zero, freeing the factory from reliance on specific individuals.
items.quote: “An organization whose memory lives inside one person's head suffers a stroke when that person takes leave.”

items.title: 4 AM Dairy Strainer
items.subtitle: The rule: Log first, deliver second
items.problem: Verbal raw milk handovers at 4 AM created massive accounting discrepancies between farmers, drivers, and silos.
items.leverIntervention: Enforcing the unshakeable rule: 'Log digitally/paper first, unload milk second' even at 4 AM.
items.results: Total elimination of milk shortages and crystal-clear farmer payment records.
items.quote: “Transparency is truly tested when enforced at 4 AM in factory darkness.”

items.title: Steak Kebab & Soda Discount
items.subtitle: Distinguishing operational profit from inflation profit
items.problem: Executives celebrated cash gains, unaware that profit stemmed from asset inflation rather than operational efficiency.
items.leverIntervention: Separating inventory inflation gains from true sales margin and revamping discount policies.
items.results: Preventing executive self-deception and safeguarding raw material purchasing power under inflation.
items.quote: “If your profit is lower than property and material inflation, you haven't made profit; you auctioned the factory.”

items.title: 24-Person Sales Team & Toxic Invoices
items.subtitle: Critiquing activity rewards versus actual results
items.problem: A 24-rep software team logged thousands of calls daily but issued uncollectible credit invoices (toxic invoices).
items.leverIntervention: Switching commission terms from 'issued invoice' to 'cash collected in bank' and filtering credit clients.
items.results: Tripled cash inflow and eliminated vanishing uncollectible invoices.
items.quote: “A sale is just a costly joke until cash hits the bank account.”

items.title: 10-Ton School Milk Distribution & Strike Scenario
items.subtitle: Crisis management 24 hours ahead of disaster
items.problem: Threatened driver strikes endangered 10 tons of pasteurized school milk in southern heat.
items.leverIntervention: Designing alternative distribution scenarios with local trucks 24 hours prior to the strike.
items.results: 100% milk delivered with zero waste, turning crisis into regional trust.
items.quote: “Crisis management means opening your umbrella before the storm, not while drowning under floods.”

cards.title: Decision Price Card
cards.subtitle: Evaluating 4 hidden costs before issuing executive orders
cards.frontSummary: Any executive decision evaluated solely on direct monetary cost imposes at least 3 hidden invisible costs on the organization.
cards.backProtocol: Before approving any project or process change, ask these 4 questions:
actionableSteps: 2. Opportunity Cost (What vital tasks are delayed while staff work on this?)
3. Learning & Error Cost (How long until operators perform without defects?)
4. Side-Effect Remediation Cost (If this fails, what is the rollback cost?)

cards.title: Internal Bleeding Diagnostic Sheet
cards.subtitle: Identifying 6 primary silent profit leak points in factories
cards.frontSummary: Internal bleeding is the slow drain of profits through voids invisible in standard financial statements.
cards.backProtocol: 6-point checklist for identifying silent leaks in warehouse & production:
actionableSteps: 1. Warehouse entry scale weight vs. waybill variance
3. Unrecorded micro-discounts granted by sales reps
4. Uncoded spare parts abandoned in warehouse shelves
6. Rework and reprocessing costs for returned goods

cards.title: 72-Hour Crisis Management Card
cards.subtitle: Prioritization protocol during abrupt resource cutoffs
cards.frontSummary: In the first 72 hours of a crisis, emotional decisions destroy organizations. The 3+ protocol focuses on protecting vital lifelines.
cards.backProtocol: Immediate 72-hour actions in order of priority:
actionableSteps: Hours 1-12: Freeze all non-essential cash outflows & verify true inventory.
Hours 12-24: Direct, transparent communication with top 3 clients & suppliers.
Hours 24-48: Activate Plan B (e.g., alternative logistics network).
Hours 48-72: Initial debrief & drafting checklists to prevent recurrence.

cards.title: Key Employee Exit Risk Card
cards.subtitle: Evaluating organizational reliance on individuals over systems
cards.frontSummary: If one employee's departure can shut down a department, you don't have a system; you have a personal fiefdom.
cards.backProtocol: 3-step formula for safeguarding against individual dependency:
actionableSteps: 1. Identify top 3 individuals holding unwritten operational knowledge.
2. Mandate video recording and checklist creation for their top 10 processes.
3. Conduct a 7-day 'No-Phone Vacation' test to evaluate system stability.

items.title: Mistaking Inflation Profit for Operational Efficiency

items.title: Log First, Deliver Second; Without Exception
